passages.t: Agur's confession, and a prayer for daily bread
passages.happening:
‘These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh’ (verse 1). He begins by confessing his weariness, ‘I am weary, O God, and worn out’ (verse 1), and his ignorance: ‘I have not learned wisdom, and I have no knowledge of the Holy One’ (verse 3).

Then he asks a string of questions. ‘Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in His hands? Who has bound up the waters in His cloak? Who has established all the ends of the earth?’ (verse 4). And what is his name, and the name of his son?

He answers with trust in God's word: “Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him” (verse 5). Do not add to his words (verse 6).

And he prays for two things before he dies. ‘Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me. Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion’ (verse 8). Too much, and he might forget God and deny him. Too little, and he might steal and dishonor God's name (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
After the long collections of Solomon's proverbs, the book turns to two voices otherwise unknown, Agur and King Lemuel. Agur appears nowhere else in Scripture. The word translated ‘burden’ in verse 1, massa, can mean a weighty pronouncement, or it may name Massa, an Arabian people descended from Ishmael, which would make Agur a sage from outside Israel. The first verse is one of the hardest in the book to translate. Older versions read names there, Ithiel and Ucal, while the BSB reads Agur's cry of weariness. Both readings are possible from the Hebrew letters.

Where earlier chapters speak with the confidence of a father, Agur begins by admitting how little he knows. Near the end of the book, his humility is a counterweight. The wisdom Proverbs offers is real, but it rests finally on God's word, not on human mastery.

Flawless is tsaraph, refined in the fire like silver with no impurity left. Verse 5 closely resembles Psalm 18:30, and verse 6 echoes Moses' command not to add to God's words.

Agur's prayer is one of the few prayers in Proverbs. He knows both dangers: wealth that makes a person forget God, and poverty that tempts a person to steal. He asks for enough.
passages.later: Agur's questions are like the ones God put to Job: ‘Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?’ (Job 38:4). The psalm says what verse 5 says: ‘the word of the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him’ (Psalm 18:30). And Moses gave the command behind verse 6: ‘You must not add to or subtract from what I command you’ (Deuteronomy 4:2).
passages.hard:
Who is the son in verse 4, and is this a prophecy of Christ?

Verse 4 asks a string of questions whose expected answer is that no human has done these things, only God: gathering the wind, binding up the waters, setting the ends of the earth in place. The last question, what is his name and the name of his son, is harder.

Readers have answered it in three main ways. Many, especially in Jewish tradition, understand the son as Israel, since God calls Israel his son (Exodus 4:22). Others think the question is an ironic challenge, like God's questions to Job: no human can name the one who does these things or claim to know his household, and the closing ‘surely you know’ exposes anyone who pretends otherwise. Many Christian interpreters have heard in the verse a glimpse of the Son who shares God's work of creation.

The verse itself does not explain the son, and the New Testament does not quote it. These notes take no side. The most careful readings let it stay an open question, one that the rest of Scripture takes up.
passages.asks: Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches. Ask which of the two dangers you are nearer to now: forgetting God in plenty, or being pushed by need toward what is wrong. And ask God for the bread that is your portion, and for the humility to know how little you know.

passages.t: Proud generations, and things never satisfied
passages.happening:
‘Do not slander a servant to his master, or he will curse you, and you will bear the guilt’ (verse 10).

Then four lines, each beginning with the word generation: a generation that curses its fathers and does not honor its mothers (verse 11); ‘a generation of those who are pure in their own eyes and yet unwashed of their filth’ (verse 12); a generation of haughty eyes (verse 13); and a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaws are knives, ‘devouring the oppressed from the earth and the needy from among men’ (verse 14).

‘The leech has two daughters: Give and Give’ (verse 15). Three things are never satisfied, and a fourth never says enough: the grave, the barren womb, land that is never satisfied with water, and fire (verses 15-16). And the eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother will come to a shameful end, left to the birds (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The four ‘generation’ lines build from disrespect to self-righteousness to pride and finally to people who devour the poor. Each step makes the next possible.

The numerical saying, a number and then that number plus one, three things, four things, was a common device in ancient wisdom. It appears in texts from Ugarit, in Amos 1 and 2, and earlier in Proverbs (6:16-19). It invites the listener to think about what the items share, and the last item usually carries the weight.

The barren womb is named among the things that long for what they do not have. It is a picture of longing, not a judgment on anyone. Many who have longed for a child, in the Bible and since, will recognize the ache it names.

The end of the mocking eye in verse 17 reflects the ancient horror of dying without burial, left exposed in an open valley. The book names it in a line, as a warning about contempt for parents.
passages.later: The book says again what verse 12 warns against: ‘All a man’s ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are weighed out by the LORD’ (Proverbs 16:2). And the psalm speaks of those who ‘devour my people like bread’ (Psalm 14:4), the generation of verse 14.
passages.asks: Agur's four generations start with disrespect and end by devouring the poor. Ask where you see yourself pure in your own eyes. And ask what in you, like the leech, keeps saying give.

passages.t: Wonders, small wise creatures, and a hand over the mouth
passages.happening:
‘There are three things too wonderful for me, four that I cannot understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a snake on a rock, the way of a ship at sea, and the way of a man with a maiden’ (verses 18-19). Then a contrast: the adulteress eats, wipes her mouth, and insists she has done nothing wrong (verse 20).

Under four things the earth trembles: a servant who becomes king, a fool who is filled with food, ‘an unloved woman who marries’, and a maidservant who takes her mistress's place (verses 21-23).

‘Four things on earth are small, yet they are exceedingly wise’ (verse 24): the ants, who store their food in summer; ‘the rock badgers are creatures of little power, yet they make their homes in the rocks’ (verse 26); ‘the locusts have no king, yet they all advance in formation’ (verse 27); and the lizard, caught in the hand, yet found in kings' palaces (verse 28). Four walk with a stately stride: the lion, the rooster, the he-goat, and a king with his army (verses 29-31).

The chapter ends with a warning. ‘If you have foolishly exalted yourself or if you have plotted evil, put your hand over your mouth’ (verse 32), for stirring up anger brings strife, as churning milk brings butter (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The four wonders in verses 18 and 19 all leave no trace, or move in ways no one can fully follow. The last, a man with a young woman, is the mystery of love. Verse 20 sets beside it a woman who betrays her marriage and leaves no trace either, or so she thinks.

Verses 21 to 23 list things that upset the social order. The unloved woman who marries is a painful picture of a marriage without love, and the book names it with sorrow, not scorn.

The animals of verses 24 to 31 were familiar. The rock badger, or hyrax, is a small animal that lives among the rocks of the Judean wilderness. Locusts moved in huge swarms that could strip a land bare, so their ordered advance without a king was both a wonder and a terror. Small and weak creatures can be wise.

Putting a hand over the mouth was a gesture of silence and shame. Agur ends where he began, humble before what he does not control.
passages.later: Job made the same gesture before God: “Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth” (Job 40:4). And Joel pictures the locusts of verse 27: ‘Each one marches in formation, not swerving from the course’ (Joel 2:7).
passages.asks: Agur learns wisdom from ants and lizards. Ask what small, ordinary thing in creation might be teaching you this week. And ask whether there is pride or a plan you need to answer by putting your hand over your mouth.
